title: The Night Before the Test
text:
The test was at eight the next morning. By ten o'clock my desk still looked like a small storm had crossed it.

My mother knocked once and left a cup of warm milk without a word. That is her [[usual]] way: no questions the night before a test.

I had read the [[whole]] chapter twice, but by then the words were sliding off the page. My eyes felt heavy and I was so [[sleepy]] that I read the same line four times without understanding any of it.

"Sleep is [[necessary]] too," my father said from the door. "A tired brain remembers nothing."

I told him I could [[hardly]] keep my eyes open, but that I still had twenty words left. He sat down on the end of the bed and asked me to say them [[aloud]]. Somehow saying them out loud made them stick.

At eleven the house went [[silent]]. My little brother had fallen [[asleep]] across his own books in the next room, and nobody moved him.

I am the kind of student who worries. Before every test I am [[nearly]] sure that I will fail, and afterwards I usually do fine. My father calls that a [[personal]] problem, not a study problem.

"Are you [[likely]] to remember more at midnight than at seven in the morning?" he asked.

I was not. I closed the book.

The next morning I woke before the alarm, ate breakfast [[alone]] in the kitchen, and walked to school in the cold air feeling strangely [[positive]]. The paper was not [[perfect]] — question eleven still bothers me — but I knew every word on it.

title: The Man Who Mends Umbrellas
topic: 人物・形容詞・老手藝
text:
Behind the wet market there is a small table with no sign on it. An old man sits there and mends umbrellas.

My grandmother has taken hers to him for thirty years. She calls him [[master]] Wu, although he laughs at the word.

His hands are not fast, but they are [[skillful]]. He opens an umbrella, turns it slowly, and finds the broken rib in about ten seconds. Then he pulls a thin wire from a box of wires, cuts it, bends it twice, and the umbrella opens smoothly again.

The tools on his table are [[ancient]]. Some of them belonged to his own teacher, who worked in this market before the war. Nothing is thrown away here: bent ribs, old handles, cloth from umbrellas beyond saving. It is a [[traditional]] way of working that almost nobody keeps now.

"Is it worth the trouble for forty dollars?" I asked him once.

He said that one umbrella is not [[valuable]], but throwing away something that still works makes him uncomfortable.

On a rainy Monday his corner is [[crowded]]. In a dry week he may sit all afternoon without one [[customer]]. His table is not [[broad]] either, so two people cannot even stand beside it at the same time.

My grandmother is one of his [[regular]] visitors. She always brings him two oranges, and he always refuses twice before taking them.

Mending umbrellas is a [[rare]] trade now, and he is [[independent]]: he has never worked for anybody in his life. Time is [[precious]] to him — he stops at six and goes home to feed his birds.

He looks like an [[ordinary]] old man with a folding stool and a box of wire. But watching those hands, I understand why my grandmother walks twenty minutes past two big shops to sit at his table.

title: Our Stall at the School Fair
text:
Our class ran a drink stall at the school fair, and Mei was my [[partner]] for the day.

Mei is no [[genius]] at math, but she counts change faster than anyone I know, so she took the money and I made the drinks. The weather was [[pleasant]] for once, not too hot.

By ten o'clock it felt as if every [[visitor]] to the fair had walked past our table. An old [[lady]] bought four cups and carried them away on a tray, very slowly. A [[gentleman]] in a grey suit asked whether we had anything without sugar, and we had not thought of that at all.

Our teacher stood behind us the whole morning like a quiet [[host]], letting us make our own mistakes.

And we made one. At eleven we ran out of ice. I felt like a complete [[fool]], standing there with warm lemon tea and a line of people waiting.

Mei did not panic. She walked over to the class next to ours, talked to them for two minutes, and came back with half a bag of ice; their stall was selling cakes, so they needed the freezer more than the ice itself. Somebody behind me said she was an [[angel]]. For the rest of that morning she was my [[hero]].

A young [[couple]] with a baby sat on the steps near us and stayed almost an hour. The father was the only [[adult]] who asked what was in the tea before buying it.

Our class has only six [[male]] students, and five of them carried tables at seven in the morning without being asked twice.

By two o'clock everything was sold. The profit was small, but the day had been [[terrific]].

Teachers keep saying that school is where you learn [[social]] skills, and I always thought that was an empty phrase. Then I spent six hours selling tea beside someone who stays calm when things go wrong. Mei and I are not [[alike]] at all, which is probably why it worked.
